messages.body_plain:
Hi John, hi listfolk,

Indeed, Eric is correct and this is possible using the plot.gam command
(in fact you can use the trans= argument to transform the values).

BUT I'd argue that this is not the right thing to do. By transforming
the plots to the response scale you start to think about looking up
values on the plot to see what the abundance effect would be -- this
doesn't quite make sense as each plot shows the effect of only one
smooth (with everything else set to zero). If you did the transformation
to the exponential (response) scale, you need to also include the offset
to be able to make the y axis make sense in this situation. In that
case, you need to add that to all of the plots to get a "prediction" for
a single point, but by adding the offset to each plot you destroy the
additive nature of the plots (as you'll add the offset multiple times).

I think it's safer to avoid this interpretation of the plots, and leave
things on the link scale.

Caveat: This kind of plot can be useful in a couple of situations:

1. when there is only 1 smooth, then the plot has a logical interpretation.
2. when the other smooths in the model (the ones that are not plotted)
can be held at a given value -- e.g., if you have a "treatment" effect
(e.g., raise in sea surface temperature of 3C) that you want to show the
effect of. In that case you still need to hold everything else constant.

I realise it's tempting to make these plots, especially when presenting
results, as it seems like it's an easy way for folks to "see" the
results. However, interpretation is tricky and in some sense the
capacity for over/misinterpretation is higher when converting to the
abundance scale. In a perverse way, it might be "safer" to stick with a
plot that no one understand and can't misinterpret than one that folks
can easily misinterpret.

Hope this helps,
--dave

Hi John, hi listfolk,

Yes, with a single smooth, you're in my point 1., below and you're fine.
I'm not sure how much information one can get from such models as given
the highly (non-linearly) correlated the covariates usually are in such
an analysis, you're likely to find some spurious results. For example,
looking at elevation may lead you to think that your study species is
interested in (say) higher areas but in fact once you include a
vegetation, you see that all the variation is taken up by that (because
the species in question really enjoys alpine trees, say).

I don't mean to trash your approach and certainly as an initial
exploratory pass through the data when you're not sure what covariates
are relevant, it's not a bad idea. But fitting models with many
covariates in and looking at the resulting smooths might give you a
better idea of what's going on.

In some sense the single covariate smooth approach will tell you what
you don't need, but it won't tell you what you definitely do.

Hope this helps.

cheers,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Fernanda

Collecting binned data means your data provide as many "points of support" as there are bins.  In your case, you have three bins.  The counts in the bins are "multinomial" meaning that if you tell me the total number of sightings (102) and the number of sightings in bins 1 (33) and 2 (31), then by subtraction I can tell you there were 38 sightings in bin 3.

As a result, the data you have collected possesses 2 degrees of freedom.

The warnings produced by Distance can be interpreted in the context of these degrees of freedom.  The first message says "number of intervals minus 1" (2 in your case) is equal to the number of key parameters in the detection function model you wish to fit (hazard rate model has 2 parameters).  Consequently, no adjustment terms can be added to the hazard rate model.  The second warning states only a single adjustment term could be added to the detection function (presumably the half normal model with a single parameter).

Finally when the goodness of fit table is produced, you see a message stating there are no degrees of freedom remaining to compute the significance of the chi-square test statistic.  Note also that the agreement between the observed and predicted values in the chi-square table is perfect.

To have a degree of freedom remaining to perform the chi-square goodness of fit test, you will need to fit a detection function that does not have two parameters (all the degrees of freedom in your data)--namely the half-normal without adjustments.

messages.subject_clean: Strip width is different than truncation distance?
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,
I'm working with data from right whale surveys in Cape Cod Bay, Massachusetts.  We have 16 lines spaced 2778 m apart, making the strip width 1389m.  However, based on the histograms of distance from trackline vs frequency of sightings, and the GOF of the models, it seems like the best truncation distance is actually left at 250m and right at 3000m (which also makes sense after flying the surveys).  I think this is the reason that my abundance estimates seem quite off.  When I have a truncation distance of 250 and 3000 the area of my covered region is larger than the actual area of the region.  I would say we quite regularly take sightings from greater than 1389m away.  I'm thinking this means we should re-work how the lines are spaced, but they have been conducting these surveys since 1998, so at this point, I would like to make the best use of the tons of data we have!

Any advice? Thanks!

~Laura Ganley
PhD student
University of Massachusetts, Boston

Sorry - follow-up.  I likely mis-understood your question.  I thought you had an estimated average detection probability of >1, but Rachel Fewster kindly pointed out to me that you likely were asking about the fact that the first two hisogram bars are at a height >1.  If that's what you're questioning then it's not a problem per se.  What happens is that Distance plots the detection function as the red line.  It then plots a histogram of the detections per bin, but it has to scale these so that the histogram and the detection function are on the same scale.  It does this by scaling the histogram bars so that the total area under the histogram is the same as the total area under the curve.  Hence, the values on the y-axis refer to the detection probability line, but are not meaningfully interpreted with respect to the histogram bars.  If you want to compare the observed number of detections with the expected number given the model, have a look at the table in the Detection Fct/Global/Chi-sq GOF Test page of the results.

By the way, if I were you, I'd right truncate your data before going much further with your analysis.  For more on truncation, see Buckland et al. (2001) Introduction to Distance Sampling, Section 2.1 or Buckland et al. (2015) Distance sampling: methods and applications, Chapter 1.

Cheers, Len

Eric

Several unusual things about your code, data, and study description.  Perhaps one (or several) of these anomalies might be causing your difficulties.  Here are my observations:

- if you data are arranged as you show, you should not need to call checkdata() and use obs, region and sample.  ds() should do all those things for you.

- Distance thinks of 'region' as strata.  The snippet of data you show has the value of region (or strata) changing for each of the 6 records you show.  That seems improbable; you should have multiple transects per strata with multiple (hopefully) detections per transect.  I suspect you are not organising your data properly.

- Your point counts have 3 distance bins from what you describe.  Because of this you can only fit very simple models-a half-normal with a single parameter, if you want to be able to test goodness-of-fit.  (see my answer on this subject to the list on 5 October 2016)

- I cannot reconcile your statement about "50 metres per plot" with your strata area or distance bins

- Left truncation of point transect data is not a good idea.

- The statement "sampling stations at 4 distances away from a different buildings" has me confused.  Were you making observations from the building (not the best idea) or were you standing at the 4 distances you describe (20, 120, 220, 320)?  If the latter, then these are not the distance bins you should use in your analysis.

Hence, the values on the y-axis refer to the detection probability line, but are not meaningfully interpreted with respect to the histogram bars.  If you want to compare the observed number of detections with the expected number given the model, have a look at the table in the Detection Fct/Global/Chi-sq GOF Test page of the results.
>
> By the way, if I were you, I'd right truncate your data before going much further with your analysis.  For more on truncation, see Buckland et al. (2001) Introduction to Distance Sampling, Section 2.1 or Buckland et al. (2015) Distance sampling: methods and applications, Chapter 1.

messages.subject: Duplicate matching in cases of species ID disagreement
messages.subject_clean: Duplicate matching in cases of species ID disagreement
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

We are having a debate about the use of between-platform duplicates in cases where the two platforms do not agree on species identity, specifically when one platform identifies species A while the other is unsure of species identity (U).

Some of us consider that species identity can and should be edited in otherwise obvious duplicate pairs using the best available data, e.g. based on observer experience, observer comments, the length of time the animal was in view etc. Others consider that if observers disagree on species identity in this way, the pair cannot be a duplicate and to edit even some AU pairs to AA based on ancillary data will negatively bias our estimate of A by increasing p(0) (because of an increase in the number of AA duplicates).

The argument against this would be that, if some of the AU pairs are in fact AA (as they very likely are), not editing them if there is evidence to do so will positively bias the estimate of A by lowering p(0).

I am wondering what other groups do in such cases.

Regards,

Daniel Pike.

messages.body_plain:
Eric

The first suspect in answer to your question noting that abundance equals number seen is perhaps that the uniform key function you fitted to your data has not required the use of the cosine adjustment term you requested.  Recognise that ds() will fit a key function without adjustment terms, then the key with adjustment terms and perform an AIC comparison between them to decide whether the adjustment is warranted.  Check to see if that is the case with your data.

Next thing to do is simply plot your data.  Does your histogram of detections by distance have the characteristic "hump" shape, or does it continue to rise at large distances?  Plotting tells you lots about where potential problems might lie.

Not sure why you are going through the pain of creating "object", "detected" and "observer" fields in your data; I trust this is single observer data.  If they are single observer data, you should be able to use the "flatfile" data format as described.  Look at the help for the Distance package under 'flatfile.'  You can also have a quick look at the supplement to the Buckland et al. (2015) book where I have reanalysed Buckland's (2006) robin point count data.

http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/DS.M&A/montrave/montrave-analysis.pdf
